failures.title: Mitsubishi 4N13 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: DPF clogging and regeneration issues
items.whatHappens: Like many modern diesels of its era, the 4N13 is highly susceptible to DPF clogging, particularly on vehicles used predominantly for short urban journeys where the DPF never reaches regeneration temperature. The 1.8‑litre displacement doesn't generate as much heat as larger diesels, making passive regeneration more difficult. Symptoms include DPF warning light, reduced power, increased fuel consumption, and limp mode.
items.repairVsReplace: DPF cleaning (around £300-£500) is usually the first step; if the DPF is damaged, replacement costs £700-£1,200. This is a maintenance issue, not a reason to replace the engine - but if left unaddressed, it can lead to turbo or engine damage. Read our full DPF failure guide

items.title: Piezo injector failure
items.whatHappens: The 4N13's piezo injectors can fail prematurely, particularly with poor‑quality fuel or irregular servicing. Symptoms include rough idle, excessive smoke, poor cold starting, and increased fuel consumption.
items.repairVsReplace: Injectors can be refurbished (around £150-£250 each) or replaced (around £300-£450 each). The 4N13's thin‑bore cylinder head can crack if injectors are removed carelessly or copper washers aren't renewed. Always use a specialist for this work.

items.title: EGR valve and cooler clogging
items.whatHappens: EGR valve and cooler carbon buildup is common on the 4N13, particularly on urban‑used vehicles. Symptoms include rough idle, hesitation, and potentially the engine entering limp mode.
items.repairVsReplace: EGR cleaning (around £200-£400) is usually sufficient; EGR cooler replacement costs around £500-£800 if it is leaking.

items.title: Timing chain tensioner wear
items.whatHappens: Some 4N13 engines have reported timing chain tensioner wear or chain stretch beyond 80,000 miles, particularly if the wrong oil has been used. The chain coordinates with the MIVEC variable valve timing system.
items.repairVsReplace: Timing chain replacement (around £700-£1,200) is the standard fix. Use the correct low‑SAPS oil (5W‑30, API CJ‑4 or equivalent) to protect the chain and DPF.

failures.goodYearsLine: The 4N13 is generally reliable when properly maintained, with no catastrophic design flaws. Later production engines (2013‑2015) benefited from improved DPF regeneration strategies and injector durability. Regular motorway driving for DPF regeneration and correct low‑SAPS oil are the key factors for longevity.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 4N13
variants.intro: The 4N13 is a specific engine code within the Mitsubishi 4N family of diesel engines. Unlike some families that fragment into many sub‑codes with different hardware, the 4N13 variants are primarily distinguished by market‑specific tuning and emissions calibration. 4N Family Overview: The 4N family includes: - 4N13 - 1.8L diesel, fitted to ASX and Lancer (this page) - 4N14 - 2.2L diesel, fitted to ASX and Outlander - 4N15 - 2.4L diesel, fitted to L200 and Shogun Sport - 4N16 - 2.4L diesel, a later variant of the 4N15 Within the 4N13, the key distinctions are: - 116 hp (85 kW) variant - standard UK market tune; 280 Nm torque - Market‑specific tuning - Some markets (Japan, Australia) received different emissions calibration (Euro 5 compliance) - FWD vs 4WD variants - In some markets, FWD and 4WD versions had different engine mount configurations, though the engine itself is identical The engine features an all‑aluminium block, DOHC 16‑valve cylinder head, common‑rail fuel system, variable‑geometry turbocharger (VGT), and MIVEC phase regulation. The MIVEC system adjusts valve timing for improved fuel economy and emissions at low RPM, and increased power at higher RPM. How to confirm your code: 1. On the engine - the 4N13 code is stamped on the engine block. Look for "4N13" on the identification plate on the front or side of the engine. 2. On the V5C logbook - the engine number is listed; cross‑reference with Mitsubishi parts systems. 3. VIN decode - use a Mitsubishi VIN decoder; the engine type will be shown. 4. Registration lookup - enter your reg above and we'll confirm the exact fitment. Similar‑looking codes it is commonly confused with: - Mitsubishi 4N14 - the 2.2‑litre version, fitted to higher‑spec ASX and Outlander; shares architecture but larger displacement and more power - Mitsubishi 4N15 - the 2.4‑litre version, fitted to L200 and Shogun Sport; the largest and most powerful 4N family member - Mitsubishi 4D56 - the 2.5‑litre predecessor in the L200; different block material and older design, not related to the 4N family

relatives.description: capacity diesels in the UK market. The petrol engines are simpler and cheaper to maintain, though less economical.

variants.closing: Why fitting the wrong revision matters: The 4N13 shares the same block architecture with the 4N14 and 4N15 but has different displacement (bore/stroke), different pistons, rods and crank, and different turbocharger specification. The 4N14 or 4N15 are not direct swaps into a 4N13‑spec vehicle without significant modifications. Always confirm the exact engine code before ordering a replacement.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 4N13 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used 4N13 makes sense for lower‑value ASX or Lancer examples where the car itself is worth under £3,000-£4,000. The key requirement is documented service history with the correct low‑SAPS 5W‑30 oil, and evidence that the DPF and injectors have been maintained. The primary risk with used units is undisclosed DPF clogging or injector wear - insist on a diagnostic scan, DPF pressure test, and injector balance check before purchase. Used units typically cost £1,200-£2,000. View used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper 4N13 recon includes DPF professional cleaning or replacement, EGR valve cleaning, injector refurbishment or replacement, timing chain tensioner inspection, new gaskets and seals, and full service with correct oil. The thin‑bore cylinder head requires specialist care during rebuild. This is the right call for most replacements - you get a like‑new unit with the known weak points already addressed, backed by 12-24 months warranty. Reconditioned units typically cost £2,500-£3,500. View reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild is justified for higher‑value, low‑mileage or well‑specified examples where originality matters. An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons, rings, bearings, timing chain kit, and a full set of gaskets. For standard applications, reconditioned is usually more cost‑effective. View rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK Mitsubishi specialists - nationwide coverage with 12‑month warranty on labour and parts. View supply & fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The 4N13 sits in compact Mitsubishi models - ASX (£2,500-£8,000), Lancer (£1,500-£6,000). A £2,500-£3,500 reconditioned engine plus £800-£1,000 fitting is a significant investment - typically 40-70% of the vehicle's value for lower‑price examples. For lower‑value examples (sub‑£3,000 ASX or Lancer), a used engine with documented DPF and injector history may be more economic. For well‑maintained, low‑mileage examples, the investment may be justified if the rest of the vehicle is in excellent condition. In many cases, however, the replacement cost approaches or exceeds the vehicle's value - evaluate carefully before committing. A thorough vehicle condition assessment is recommended.

items.question: What are the common problems with the Mitsubishi 4N13 engine?
items.answer: The 4N13's most common issues are DPF clogging (particularly with urban driving), piezo injector failure (often fuel-quality related), EGR valve carbon buildup, and timing chain tensioner wear at higher mileages. The engine is generally reliable when properly maintained but requires regular DPF regeneration. DPF cleaning is essential for urban vehicles. Injector failure causes rough running and excessive smoke. Regular motorway driving helps DPF regeneration.

items.question: Is the 4N13 a reliable engine?
items.answer: The 4N13 is generally reliable when properly maintained, but the DPF system requires regular motorway driving for passive regeneration. The 1.8-litre displacement doesn't generate enough heat for passive regeneration during short urban trips, making this the engine's single biggest weakness. With regular maintenance (correct low-SAPS oil, good fuel quality, occasional motorway runs), the engine can exceed 150,000 miles. DPF regeneration requires regular motorway driving. Use of low-SAPS 5W-30 oil is essential. Good fuel quality prevents injector wear.
